newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lawyers oppose California ballot plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lawyers oppose California ballot plan.

text.p: The Clinton administration argued on Wednesday that California's recently approved ballot initiative aimed at dismantling affirmative action programmes was unconstitutional and should not be allowed to take effect.
Justice Department lawyers, laying out their arguments against the measure for the first time, said the new law should remain suspended while the case is on appeal.
A federal judge in San Francisco has temporarily blocked enforcement of the ballot initiative, known as Proposition 209, because of a "strong possibility" it will be held unconstitutional.
California Gov. Pete Wilson, a Republican who strongly backed the initiative, said the Clinton administration's filing was "deeply regrettable."

In a 28-page document filed with a U.S. appeals court in California, department lawyers opposed a request by the state seeking to lift the judge's order and allow the measure to go into effect while the legal battle goes forward.

"Once the district court's order is lifted, Proposition 209 will be binding state law; any affirmative action programme that violates Proposition 209 may be immediately terminated," Acting Assistant Attorney General Isabelle Katz Pinzler said.

"Proposition 209 is unconstitutional because it singles out racial and gender issues for unique treatment in the political process and thereby burdens the enactment of legislation designed to overcome prejudice," she said.

The measure bars discrimination and preferential treatment based on race or sex in public employment, education and contracting in California, effectively outlawing government affirmative action programmes used to broaden opportunities for women and minorities.
The administration announced last month it would join the court fight against the law, which was approved by 54 percent of the California voters Nov. 5.

President Clinton has expressed opposition to the measure, preferring instead his own "mend it, not end it" prescription for reforming affirmative action programmes aimed at giving minorities and women equal job opportunities.
Pinzler cited Supreme Court rulings from 1969 and 1982 in arguing against the law.
She said states have the authority to decide whether to adopt affirmative action programmes or to repeal such programmes. But she said the California measure went too far.

"Not only does Proposition 209 single out programmes designed to overcome prejudice, it also effectively limits the access of minorities and women -- the primary beneficiaries of affirmative action -- to the levers of government," she said.

Pinzler said the law placed an unfair burden on women and minorities seeking lawful affirmative action programmes, requiring that they took the "extraordinarily difficult" step of amending the state constitution.
The appeals court has scheduled a hearing in the case for Feb. 10, a Justice Department spokesman said.
